title: CERN Begins Swapping Out Magnets in the Large Hadron Collider
summary:
The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) — a 27-kilometer ring buried beneath France and Switzerland — is getting a major upgrade. On September 7, CERN crews began dismantling sections of the collider on either side of its ATLAS and CMS experiments, formally starting the replacement of 28 superconducting magnets. The work is happening during the machine's third long shutdown, known as LS3, and crews began by cutting the first magnet interconnection. CERN Director-General Mark Thomson visited LHC Point 1, home of the ATLAS experiment, to mark the milestone.

The LHC relies on thousands of magnets to steer and focus its particle beams. Among the most important are the inner triplets — groups of three quadrupole magnets that sit on both sides of the LHC's four main experiments. Their job is to squeeze the beams as tightly as possible just before particles collide. The tighter the squeeze, the greater the chance of collisions, which increases the LHC's luminosity — the number of collisions in a given period. More luminosity means more data.

The upgrade is part of the High-Luminosity LHC (HiLumi LHC) project. The new inner triplets use niobium-tin superconducting coils instead of niobium-titanium, allowing them to generate magnetic fields reaching 11.3 tesla — about 40% stronger than the current magnets. They'll be installed around ATLAS and CMS, where the higher collision rate matters most. ALICE and LHCb don't need the same increase, but their magnets will still be upgraded to benefit from the overall boost.

The current inner triplets date back to the LHC's construction and were installed between 2005 and 2007. "After nearly twenty years of operation, they will give way to a new generation of even more powerful magnets," said Markus Zerlauth, the HiLumi LHC project leader. "It's truly remarkable to witness such a handover from one generation of innovation to the next."

In total, 16 cryostats and 28 cryo-assemblies will be installed — what Jean-Philippe Tock, head of the LS3 Coordination Team, calls "a major undertaking." The first quadrupole of the new triplets should arrive in the tunnel at the start of 2029.
why_it_matters: Particle physics is a long game: questions about what the universe is made of are not answered in a single experiment, and this upgrade decides whether the LHC collects enough collisions to catch extremely rare processes — possibly hints of physics beyond the particles we already know. It is also a lesson in how big science works, through decades of engineering, international funding and patience.

background_read: CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research, the world's largest particle-physics laboratory, based near Geneva on the French–Swiss border) built the Large Hadron Collider, which first circulated its beams in 2008.

The LHC's most famous result came in 2012, when the ATLAS and CMS experiments (two giant detectors built around the points where beams collide) announced the discovery of the Higgs boson, the particle tied to why other particles have mass.

Accelerators work by pushing particles to nearly the speed of light and smashing them together; the more collisions a machine produces, the more rare and fleeting events physicists can catch, which is why upgrades often focus on collision rate as much as raw energy.

Magnets are usually the bottleneck. Existing niobium-titanium coils have a practical field limit, so reaching higher fields requires new materials such as niobium-tin, kept near absolute zero inside cryostats filled with liquid helium.
The High-Luminosity LHC is designed to pile up far more collision data than the current machine over its lifetime, extending the search for physics beyond the particles we already know.

perspectives.description: Physicists gain a machine that produces far more collisions, which is the only way to spot very rare events. The switch to niobium-tin coils also pushes superconducting technology forward, with possible spin-offs for medicine and future accelerators.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — huge cost, years without collisions
perspectives.description: Long shutdowns mean the LHC cannot run for years, and the upgrade carries a very large price tag funded by many countries. Some critics ask whether the returns justify the spending, especially since the LHC has so far found no clear signs of new particles beyond the Higgs boson.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — a normal cycle in big science
perspectives.description: Every major accelerator goes through shutdowns and upgrades; it is how machines stay at the research frontier. The move from niobium-titanium to niobium-tin magnets follows a familiar pattern in technology, where new materials unlock the next level of performance.

The first new quadrupole should reach the tunnel around the start of 2029, so the real scientific payoff will come well after today's students finish school. Whether it reveals new physics, or simply sharpens measurements of known particles, depends on data that does not yet exist.
